moles-molar-mass-s2.title: A box of molecules
moles-molar-mass-s2.html: Key: large dark circle, oxygen atom; small light circle, hydrogen atom.

items.q: How many moles of carbon dioxide are in Sample 2?

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied the mass by the molar mass. Divide instead, so grams cancel and moles are left.

why.correct: 22.0 g × (1 mol / 44.01 g) = 0.49989 mol, which is 0.500 mol to the three significant figures of the mass.

items.q: Which sample contains the greatest number of molecules?
options: Sample 1, the water
Sample 2, the carbon dioxide
Sample 3, the methane
Sample 4, the glucose

why.correct: The number of molecules follows the number of moles. Sample 1 holds 36.0 / 18.02 = 2.00 mol; the other three hold about 0.500 mol each.
options: Right: 2.00 mol of water, four times the amount in each other sample.
About 0.500 mol: a larger mass than the methane, but a heavier molecule.
About 0.499 mol: the smallest mass, but also the lightest molecule, so it is close to the others.
The largest mass, but each molecule is heavy, so it is only about 0.500 mol.

items.q: Samples 2 and 4 hold nearly the same amount in moles, yet Sample 4 has about four times the mass. Which statement explains this?
options: Each glucose molecule has about four times the mass of a carbon dioxide molecule.
Glucose molecules are packed more tightly, so more of them fit in the sample.
Carbon dioxide molecules lose some mass when they are weighed as a gas.
A mole of glucose holds four times as many molecules as a mole of carbon dioxide.

why.correct: Equal moles means equal numbers of molecules. The mass ratio then comes from the mass of one molecule: 180.16 / 44.01 is about 4.1.
options: Right: same number of molecules, each about 4.1 times heavier.
Packing changes the volume a sample takes up, not its mass per molecule or the count per mole.
Mass does not depend on how the substance is held; a weighed gas has its full mass.
Every mole holds 6.022 × 10²³ particles, whatever the substance.

items.q: How many molecules of methane are in Sample 3? Give your answer in scientific notation.

why.correct: 8.00 g × (1 mol / 16.04 g) = 0.4988 mol; 0.4988 mol × 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 3.00 × 10²³ molecules.

items.q: How many atoms are shown in the box?

why.correct: Six molecules, each made of three atoms (one oxygen, two hydrogen): 6 × 3 = 18 atoms.

items.q: Which statement describes what the box holds?
options: One compound: every molecule has the same two elements in the same ratio.
One element: each particle in the box is made of the same atom.
Two elements mixed together: oxygen atoms and separate hydrogen atoms.
Two compounds: the oxygen atoms and hydrogen atoms form different substances.

why.correct: All six molecules are identical, and each joins two different elements in a fixed 2 : 1 ratio, so the box holds one compound.
options: Right: one kind of molecule, two elements, fixed ratio.
Each molecule holds two kinds of atom, so the substance is not an element.
The hydrogen atoms are bonded to oxygen inside each molecule, not loose beside it.
Every molecule is the same, so there is only one substance in the box.

items.q: Suppose each molecule drawn stood for 1.00 mol of molecules. What would the mass of the sample be?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided the moles by the molar mass. Moles times grams per mole gives grams.

why.correct: 6.00 mol × 18.02 g/mol = 108.12 g, which is 108 g to three significant figures.

items.q: How many moles of hydrogen atoms are in one mole of the substance in the box?
options: 1 mol
2 mol
3 mol
6 mol

why.correct: Each molecule holds two hydrogen atoms, so one mole of molecules holds two moles of hydrogen atoms.
options: One is the number of oxygen atoms in each molecule.
Right: two hydrogen atoms in every molecule.
Three is the number of atoms of both kinds in each molecule.
Six is the number of molecules drawn, not a count per molecule.

items.q: What does the molar mass of a substance tell you?
options: The mass of one mole of it, in grams
The number of atoms in one molecule of it
The mass of one molecule of it, in grams
The number of moles in one gram of it

why.correct: Molar mass is grams per mole: the mass of 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
options: Right: grams per mole.
That is a count of atoms, which the molecular picture gives.
One molecule weighs about 10⁻²³ g; the molar mass is the mass of a whole mole.
That is the inverse, moles per gram.

items.q: Nitrogen has an atomic mass of 14.01 and hydrogen 1.008. What is the molar mass of a molecule with one nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms?
options: 15.02 g/mol
17.03 g/mol
43.04 g/mol
45.05 g/mol

why.correct: Add the atomic mass of every atom: 14.01 + 3(1.008) = 17.03 g/mol.
options: This counts only one hydrogen atom.
Right: one nitrogen and three hydrogens.
This counts three nitrogen atoms and one hydrogen atom.
This counts three of each atom.

items.q: What is the mass of 0.0450 mol of water (molar mass 18.02 g/mol)?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided by the molar mass. To go from moles to grams, multiply by grams per mole.

why.correct: 0.0450 mol × 18.02 g/mol = 0.8109 g, which is 0.811 g to three significant figures.

items.q: Which quantities are equal to one mole of water molecules?
options: 6.022 × 10²³ water molecules
18.02 g of water
1.008 g of water
6.022 × 10²³ atoms of hydrogen and oxygen

why.correct: A mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles, and its mass in grams is the molar mass, 18.02 g for water.
options: Right: the definition of a mole of molecules.
Right: the molar mass of water.
That is the atomic mass of hydrogen, not the molar mass of water.
Each molecule has three atoms, so a mole of molecules holds three moles of atoms.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the number of molecules in a weighed sample in order.
options: Write down the measured mass in grams
Divide by the molar mass to get moles
Multiply by Avogadro's number to get molecules
Round to the significant figures of the mass

why.correct: Grams to moles with the molar mass, moles to molecules with Avogadro's number, then round once at the end.

options: The number of particles in one mole
The mass of one mole of carbon atoms
The number of atoms in one molecule
The mass of one atom in grams

why.correct: Avogadro's number, 6.022 × 10²³, is how many particles make one mole.
options: Right: 6.022 × 10²³ particles per mole.
That is the molar mass of carbon, 12.01 g.
Atoms per molecule depends on the molecule.
Atoms weigh about 10⁻²³ g each; this number is a count, not a mass.

items.q: A student reports that 36.0 g of water is 649 mol. Which error best explains this result?
options: The mass was multiplied by the molar mass.
The mass was divided by Avogadro's number.
The molar mass was rounded to 18.0 g/mol.
The mass was recorded with too few digits.

why.correct: 36.0 × 18.02 = 649. Dividing gives the right answer, 2.00 mol; an estimate (36 g is about twice 18 g) catches the slip.
options: That would give a tiny number, about 6 × 10⁻²³.
Rounding the molar mass changes the answer in the third digit, not by a factor of 300.
Too few digits changes the precision, not the size, of the answer.
